findings.claim: Grok placeholder reply becomes usable when a turn reads then emits no post-tool text: final_text is empty, so the whole-stream text (the pre-read placeholder) is used and ok=true, bypassing the zero-tool guard because tool_calls>0.

evidence.observation: reply falls back to events.text when final_text is empty despite tool_calls>0; guard only fires at 0 calls in run_detailed.

findings.remedy: When tool_calls>0 and final_text is blank, fail the turn (empty final answer) instead of falling back to whole-stream text; keep whole text only as salvage.
findings.trigger: text placeholder, then tool_call, then end_turn with no later text event.
findings.verification: Unit-test read_grok_events/grok_turn_outcome with that stream; expect not ok and no usable reply.

findings.claim: Pass lock acquisition is racy: existence is checked then the lock is written with plain fs::write, so two concurrent passes can both acquire and update simultaneously.

evidence.observation: acquire_lock reads/checks pid_alive then fs::write overwrites; no create_new/O_EXCL or compare-and-swap. hook_line also checks lock_held before spawning, widening the race.

findings.remedy: Create the lock with create_new(true); on contention re-read and only take over a proven-dead lock via an atomic replace protocol.
findings.trigger: Two SessionStart hooks, or hook plus manual --run, start at the same time.
findings.verification: Spawn two maintain passes concurrently against fake CLIs and assert only one runs updates.

findings.claim: In-use protection is only a name match checked once before a minutes-long smoke/update, so an engine can be updated while in use.

evidence.observation: engine_in_use matches only process-name stem to launcher stem and comments that read failure means not-in-use; maintain_one_engine checks it once then smokes and updates much later with no recheck. Model swaps in run_models have no in-use check at all.

findings.remedy: Re-check immediately before do_update and before apply_swap using the live-run registry/pids as well as process names; skip and retry tomorrow on any doubt, including enumeration failure for updatable engines.
findings.trigger: A consultation starts after the in-use scan but before npm/grok/kimi update, or the engine runs via node/cmd/powershell so its process name differs from the launcher stem.
findings.verification: Fake-CLI test that starts a matching live process mid-smoke and asserts no update/swap occurs.

findings.claim: When the installed version cannot be parsed, the pass still updates and then tries to roll back to the literal string unknown, leaving a failed-smoke version installed despite an existing rollback path; rollback success is also never verified by re-reading/re-smoking.

evidence.observation: installed_text becomes "unknown"; the up-to-date guard requires Some(inst); do_rollback is called with installed_text; success is taken from exit code only.

findings.remedy: Hold the update when installed is unknown; after rollback re-read the version, require equality with the previous version, and re-smoke or report rollback-unverified.
findings.trigger: --version output has no parseable semver token, update succeeds, post-update smoke fails.
findings.verification: Fake pass with unparseable installed version and failing post-update smoke; assert no update is attempted.

findings.claim: Grok update is unpinned, so it can install a version newer than the checked latest (and newer than any cool-down assessment) in a check/update race.

evidence.observation: check_grok returns latestVersion with released=None, so min-age never applies to grok; do_update runs plain `grok update` and ignores the `to` argument, unlike codex/kimi pins.

findings.remedy: Use `grok update --version <checked>` for the update, or re-check after update and roll back when the installed version differs from the checked one.
findings.trigger: A new grok release appears between `grok update --check` and `grok update`.
findings.verification: Fake grok whose update installs a different version than --check reported; assert the pass rejects/rolls it back.

findings.claim: A hostile or malformed model id from a model-list endpoint/CLI can break out of the roster JSON string because the successor id is spliced unescaped and validation only checks that the result loads.

evidence.observation: parse_models_json accepts arbitrary id strings; replace_entry_model inserts `new` raw between quotes; apply_swap validates loadability but does not verify exactly one intended field changed or that the parsed model equals `new`.

findings.remedy: Reject model ids outside a strict charset before candidacy, JSON-escape on splice, and post-validate that the parsed roster differs in exactly the target entry's model.
findings.trigger: /v1/models or `grok models` returns an id containing a quote/backslash/newline crafted to remain parseable.
findings.verification: apply_swap/replace_entry_model test with a quote-bearing successor; expect refusal and an unchanged roster.

findings.claim: The never-swap stamped-id rule is bypassable: a dotted date/build suffix is parsed as the model version itself.

evidence.observation: is_stamped only rejects a final -// segment that is all digits of length >=3; parse_model_id takes the LAST digits.digits run, so model-5.3-2026.11 is treated as major 2026/minor 11 and a later date becomes its successor.

findings.remedy: Reject ids with any trailing date/build-like segment (including dotted dates) and require the version run to be the model version, not a suffix stamp; add successor tests for dotted-date ids.
findings.trigger: Seated model-5.3-2026.11 with candidate model-5.3-2026.12 in the same source list.

findings.claim: Roster swaps can silently overwrite a concurrent roster edit: apply_swap reads, validates and writes with no lock, mtime or content check.

evidence.observation: apply_swap reads the file, optionally backs it up, validates the edited string, then fs::write replaces the path; nothing detects that the file changed after the read.

findings.remedy: Hold the roster/commit lock during read-edit-write or compare the on-disk content/hash immediately before writing and abort on change.
findings.trigger: Operator or another c3 process edits the roster between apply_swap's read and write (the smoke window makes this minutes long).
findings.verification: Test that mutates the roster file after the backup/read step and asserts apply_swap refuses to write.

findings.claim: A read-insist re-ask that never actually ran (LaunchFailed, 0 tool calls) is recorded as the dead attempt that ended the run, and when its salvage is empty the reply record still holds the primary placeholder.

evidence.observation: Any non-Completed outcome breaks the loop as ReaskDeath regardless of tool calls; raw_text is replaced only when salvage is non-empty. grok_salvage also concatenates all text events, including pre-tool interim text.

findings.remedy: Only treat a re-ask as the dead reviewing attempt when it made tool calls or produced an engine-classified failure; otherwise keep the guard outcome/retry, and use final_text-based salvage.
findings.trigger: Fresh grok re-ask fails to launch, or dies with no salvaged text after a zero-tool primary.
findings.verification: Fake-grok test with FAKE_GROK_RESUME_NO_END plus a launch-failure variant; assert outcome, final_tool_calls and reply file name the correct attempt.

findings.claim: Budget live sources share one cache file per plan and past-reset live windows are never marked stale, so the panel can be fed another source's empty result or a pre-reset usage figure.

evidence.observation: cache_path is only .cache-{plan}.json for kimi/zai/muse; zai/muse/kimi windows set observed_at=now and stale=false even when resets_at is already past, unlike snapshot staleness at resets_at<=now.

findings.remedy: Key caches by source+plan and drop/mark stale any window whose resets_at<=now before multiplier/display use.
findings.trigger: Two vendors share a plan slug, or a cached zai/muse window crosses its reset within the 300 s cache life.
findings.verification: Unit tests: same-plan kimi cache must not suppress the muse probe; a past-reset TOKENS_LIMIT yields no governing window.

findings.claim: Maintenance child processes, including the downloaded kimi installer and npm install scripts, inherit the operator's full environment (minus host markers), exposing API keys to third-party install code.

evidence.observation: SystemEnv::run builds Command from the inherited environment, scrubs only host markers, then runs npm/grok/kimi installer with that environment; the kimi script is executed with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass.

findings.remedy: Run update/install commands with a minimal allowlisted environment (PATH, home, temp, installer pin only), explicitly removing provider/API key variables.
findings.trigger: Any maintain update on a machine whose shell/hook environment contains ZAI_API_KEY, KIMI_API_KEY, xAI or cloud credentials.
findings.verification: Fake installer that dumps its environment; assert no provider key names/values are present.

findings.claim: The claimed --smoke/no-state invariant is not literal: a non-dry --smoke creates its scratch repo under the maintain state directory, and kimi redirects accept any subdomain of the registrable site.

evidence.observation: run_one_smoke builds work under the state dir and run_consult_smoke creates it (removed afterwards, but the state dir remains); redirect_target compares only the last two host labels, so code.kimi.ai may redirect to any *.kimi.ai host whose script is then executed.

findings.remedy: Use the OS temp dir for smoke scratch; pin kimi redirects to an allowlist (code.kimi.ai/cdn.kimi.ai) rather than the whole registrable domain.
findings.trigger: `c3 maintain --smoke` on a fresh home; or a kimi CDN redirect to a different kimi.ai subdomain.
findings.verification: Assert no maintain directory is created by --smoke, and redirect_target refuses a non-allowlisted kimi.ai subdomain.

first_run_checklist: Watch the first detached pass end-to-end: lock appears once, state.json advances last_pass/next_due once, and the report is printed exactly once by a later hook.
Before/after each engine update record --version, the smoke result and, on any post-update smoke failure, proof the re-read version equals the pre-update version.
Diff the roster against its .bak-maintain-<date> backup: exactly one model value may differ, on the intended provider entry.
Confirm no engine with a live consultation/process was updated and no swap was seated while its plan window was saturated.
Check last-run.log and state for kimi/npm/grok child output containing no API-key values and no unexpected redirect host.
reply_markdown:
Verdict: **HOLD** — do not commit/install 0.2.4 until findings #1, #4, #6 and #11 are fixed; the wave is default-on and touches binaries, roster and credentials.

**Q1. Maintain pass.** Install-without-smoke is mostly guarded, but: concurrent passes can both take the lock (finding #2); in-use is a process-name match checked once, minutes before the update, and never for model swaps (#3); an unparseable installed version still updates and rolls back to `unknown`, with rollback never re-verified (#4); grok's update is unpinned, so a release landing between check and update installs unchecked (#5); a crash before the final state write re-runs the pass next session (idempotent for versions, costly in smokes).

**Q2. Roster swap.** Sound in the normal case (same prefix/suffix/major, higher minor; backup; re-parse), but a hostile model id is spliced into the JSON unescaped and validation only proves it loads (#6); dotted-date stamped ids evade the never-swap rule (#7); concurrent roster edits are silently overwritten (#8). `position` is recorded but unused — provider+model disambiguation is the only guard.

**Q3. Security.** Worst: npm/grok/kimi installer children inherit the full environment, so install scripts can read plan/API keys (#11). Command injection via version strings is well contained (argv, numeric-only versions), but model ids reach the roster unsanitised (#6), the kimi script is download-and-run by design with redirects allowed to any `*.kimi.ai` subdomain (#12), and keyed model-list GETs correctly refuse redirects.

**Q4. Grok.** Fresh-conversation re-asks, thread clearing and dead-re-ask naming are correctly wired, except: a read followed by no post-tool text resurrects the pre-read placeholder as a usable reply (#1), and a re-ask that never launched is recorded as the dead attempt while the placeholder remains the reply of record (#9).

**Q5. Budget.** Units check out (percent via `finite_percent`, epoch-ms, TIME_LIMIT ignored, null allowance yields nothing), but caches collide across sources per plan slug and past-reset live windows stay non-stale, so the draw can use a wrong/empty window (#10).

**Q6. Untested.** No live update, rollback, kimi installer or roster swap (per the brief); no tests for lock contention, mid-pass engine start, unknown-version rollback, hostile model ids, the grok no-final-text stream, or cross-vendor plan collisions; the c3-cli integration suite has not yet completed cleanly (one preflight timeout under load).

## Requested checks
- RC1 (read-only, `crates/c3-cli`): rerun the full integration suite single-threaded on an idle machine; a clean pass settles finding #9's harness coverage. Budget: one suite run.
- RC2 (workspace-write, scratch home): fake-grok stream with placeholder text, one tool call, no final text; observing a usable reply confirms finding #1. Budget: minutes.
unproven: A real engine update, rollback, kimi installer run and roster swap have never been exercised live (stated in the brief).
The full c3-cli integration suite has not completed: its first pass stopped on a claude --version preflight timeout under load.
Whether z.ai returns more than one TOKENS_LIMIT item, and whether real roster plan slugs collide across vendors, was not verified against live responses.
pid_alive behaviour with an empty start_time in a stale lock was not inspected in the liveness implementation.
verdict_reason: Default-on auto-update can seat a placeholder Grok reply as usable, roll back to an unknown version, splice unsanitised model ids into the roster, and expose API keys to installer scripts.
